Interoperability with other formats

Source: vignettes/rwl-export.Rmd
rwl-export.Rmd
library(rxs2tria)

Overview

Annually resolved QWA parameters are time series like ring widths, and can be analysed with standard dendrochronological tools. rxs2tria currently connects to them at three levels:

  • dplR: extract_rwl() builds an rwl object (years as row names, one column per woodpiece) from a chosen parameter from the rings data or a sector profile at a givensector. This is the format established by the dplR package, and can thus be used as the basis for all its capabilities (e.g. for detrending and chronology building).
  • Tucson .rwl files: the classic exchange format, read e.g. by COFECHA, is restrictive about series IDs and value ranges. rename_for_tucson() and scale_for_tucson() prepare the rwl object for dplR::write.tucson().
  • TSAP: write_tsap() writes a tab-delimited file for import into TSAP, after scale_for_tsap() where needed.

Creating a dplR rwl object

Prerequisites

extract_rwl() takes the $rings component of a QWAdata object after complete_QWAdata(), which adds the ring flags the export relies on (see vignette("workflow")). If you review ring quality in the flags app (vignette("flags-app")), extract the series after flagging.

Which years are included

Each woodpiece yields one series, with its woodpiece_label as column name. Two kinds of rings are removed before building the series:

  • duplicate rings not selected as the preferred copy (exclude_dupl),
  • rings flagged for exclusion (exclude_issues).

NA flags count as FALSE. Years of removed rings become NA measurement values, and each series spans the full year range of the rwl object, so gaps are explicit. If more than one ring per woodpiece and year remains, the function aborts; check the exclude_dupl flags of the reported woodpieces.

Ring parameters

Any measurement column of the rings data (e.g. mrw, eww, lww, ra) can be exported directly:

rwl_mrw <- extract_rwl(df_rings = QWA_data$rings, param = "mrw")

Profile parameters

Aggregated cell parameters come from a sector profile (see vignette("QWAprofile")). Pass the profile as prf_data and select a sector; param must be a mean or quantile measurement aggreagate column of the profile (e.g. la_mean, la_q90):

prf_sector <- calculate_sector_profiles(
  QWA_data,
  n_sectors        = 5,
  sel_cell_params  = c("la", "cwtrad"),
  quant_probs      = c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9)
)

rwl_la <- extract_rwl(df_rings = QWA_data$rings, param = "la_q90",
                      prf_data = prf_sector, sector = 5)

The exclusion flags are always read from df_rings, so it is required in both cases. The profile must be computed from the same QWAdata object after complete_QWAdata(); profile years without a rings row abort the extraction.

Affected tissue: By default, every value from a ring with exclude_issues is removed by extract_rwl. However, in the flags app (vignette("flags-app")) you may have filled in the affected_tissue column to indicate that for some exclude_issues rings, only the latewood or earlywood part of the tissue may actually be affected. In that case, it is possilbe to calculate the sector aggregates on the unaffected tissue cells only, with apply_exclusions = TRUE and tissue = "affected". Then aggregates from rings whose issue only affects the earlywood or latewood (affected_tissue "ew" or "lw") are kept, using the values of the unaffected tissue. In the rwl extraction, you can then relax the ring exclusion criteria analogously to keep the values from aggregates of unaffected cells in excluded rings.

prf_sector <- calculate_sector_profiles(
  QWA_data,
  n_sectors        = 5,
  sel_cell_params  = c("la", "cwtrad"),
  apply_exclusions = TRUE, # already filter out rings with exclude_* here
  tissue           = "affected" # exclude only cells from affected tissue
)

rwl_cwt <- extract_rwl(df_rings = QWA_data$rings, param = "cwtrad_mean",
                       prf_data = prf_sector, sector = 5,
                       tissue = "affected")

Working with dplR

The result is a regular dplR rwl object, so the dplR functions apply directly, e.g.:

dplR::rwl.report(rwl_mrw)
summary(rwl_mrw)

rwi <- dplR::detrend(rwl_mrw, method = "AgeDepSpline")
crn <- dplR::chron(rwi)

The values keep the units of the QWA data (e.g. µm for ring widths, µm² for lumen area), and the column names are the woodpiece_labels. See https://opendendro.github.io/learningToLoveDplR for more info.

Writing Tucson .rwl files

Tucson .rwl files are a widely supported exchange format for ring-width series, read e.g. by COFECHA. The format imposes two constraints on the rwl object:

  • Series IDs of at most 6 characters (7-8 with long.names = TRUE), out of A-Z, a-z and 0-9.
  • Values stored as integers at a precision prec of 0.001 or 0.01, with 5 digits of usable range.

Series IDs

woodpiece_labels usually exceed the ID length. dplR::write.tucson() would truncate them; rename_for_tucson() instead derives short IDs from the data structure, using the first of these variants that is unique and short enough for all series:

  1. site label + base ID (e.g. YAM_LASI_122_a → YAM122a),
  2. base ID only (122a),
  3. species code + base ID (LASI122a).

The base ID is the woodpiece_label without the site and species prefixes, reduced to the allowed characters. The data structure columns (woodpiece_label, site_label, optionally species_code) are taken from a QWAimages object, e.g. rxs_images or QWA_meta$images. Pass the same long.names value you will use when writing:

rwl_out <- rename_for_tucson(rwl_mrw, rxs_images, long.names = TRUE)
attr(rwl_out, "mapping")

The mapping from woodpiece_label to series ID is stored in the "mapping" attribute. To preview the IDs without renaming, use make_short_series_ids(rxs_images, max_chars = 8). If no unique mapping can be derived, the function aborts.

Scaling

scale_for_tucson() multiplies all values by a power of ten. ROXAS (AI) ring widths are measured in µm, while dplR::write.tucson conventioally expects mm (written back to µm at precision 0.001 in the actual Tucson file), so use scaling = 0.001 for mrw, eww and lww:

rwl_out <- scale_for_tucson(rwl_out, prec = 0.001, scaling = 0.001)

For other parameters, leave scaling = NULL to choose the largest factor that keeps all values within the 5-digit range at the given prec:

rwl_la_out <- rwl_la |>
  rename_for_tucson(rxs_images, long.names = TRUE) |>
  scale_for_tucson(prec = 0.001)
attr(rwl_la_out, "scaling")

A manual scaling that pushes values beyond the range aborts, with the largest factor that fits as hint.

Writing

Call dplR::write.tucson() with the same prec and long.names:

dplR::write.tucson(rwl_out, fname = "mrw.rwl", prec = 0.001,
                   long.names = TRUE)

Note that dplR::write.tucson() had a recent version change. Before version 1.8.0, missing and negative values are written automatically to 0, while in the newer versions, these values are replaced by the missing value marker 999, which may lead to issues in COFECHA. use the parameter fill.internal.NA = 0 to establish the old behaviour, cf. https://opendendro.org/r/#new-in-180.

Writing TSAP import files

write_tsap() writes a tab-delimited text file for import into TSAP: a Year column followed by one column per series, named by woodpiece_label. Values are rounded to integers (since the standard import settings in TSAP do not allow for decimal digits), and missing values are written as 0.

TSAP typically expects ring widths in µm, so mrw, eww and lww can be written as they are:

write_tsap(rwl_mrw, "mrw_tsap.txt")

Parameters on smaller scales (e.g. cell wall thickness, relative measures) would lose most of their information when rounded. Scale them first with scale_for_tsap(), which by default picks the largest power of ten keeping all values at most 9999:

rwl_cwt_out <- scale_for_tsap(rwl_cwt)
attr(rwl_cwt_out, "scaling")
write_tsap(rwl_cwt_out, "cwttan_mean_tsap.txt")

write_tsap() warns if non-zero values round to 0. As missing values are also written as 0, gaps from excluded rings cannot be told apart from zero-width (missing) rings in the TSAP file.

What to keep in mind

  • Apply the preparation functions last. The "scaling" and "mapping" attributes are kept by rename_for_tucson() and scale_for_tucson() (so either order works), but dropped by most other operations (subsetting, arithmetic, dplR functions). An object that already carries the attribute is not scaled or renamed again.

  • Record the scaling factor and ID mapping. Neither is stored in the written files. Divide the exported values by scaling to recover the original values (up to rounding). For the raw integers in a Tucson file, apply * prec / scaling instead; values re-read with dplR::read.tucson() only need / scaling. To keep the mapping, e.g.:

    write.csv(attr(rwl_out, "mapping"), "mrw_series_ids.csv",
          row.names = FALSE)

  • Long-format alternative. For further analyses in R, use extract_ring_measures(): it returns the ring measurements with the same rings removed, one row per woodpiece and year.
